title: Six weeks from release, and almost no marketing.  What should I be doing?
author: CraigBMG
selftext:
I'm a solo developer, getting ready to release *Jigsaw Diorama: The Alchemist and the Eclipse* on Steam. It's a relaxing jigsaw puzzle game with sixteen steampunk-fantasy-inspired scenes, connected through an implied story and journey.

The game was prototyped without AI, with the intention of using animated 3D scenes for the puzzle times.  However, the content creation time and the performance implications were proving too much to overcome, so I went with AI generated (and heavily edited) stills to actually get something to completion.

The game itself is basically done, but I haven't spent any time on marketing yet.  I have mostly been dreading running into anti-AI backlash.

I've been considering creating additional trailers, short clips, relaxing or ambient puzzle-completion videos, and doing a small amount of paid advertising. 

For anyone who has launched a game on Steam, what was actually worth the time or money?

comments.author: account009988
comments.body: All the images are AI. People hate ai. Good luck

comments.author: theflossboss1
comments.body: You are toast.  That much AI usage will garner a ton of hate from the pc audience.  You will probably want to change your “Developed by” account on Steam so you don’t mess up your future game publicity.

comments.author: -svde-
comments.body:
you should probably be marketing. have you tried marketing? i think marketing might help.

in all seriousness, you spent all this time and effort apparently creating this game, why would you trash all of that just to “get something to completion”? what made you think you needed to rush things and make it worse by virtue of removing the human element, which is the WHOLE POINT of puzzles?

idk what you mean by "performance implications", but the whole rushing thing is one of the things that drives me the most nuts when it comes to vibed shit. what self-imposed deadline made you betray your own project's integrity?

if you were so concerned about anti AI backlash, why in the world didn't you just invest the money you intend to spend on paid adverts on *real art*? you could have commissioned a handful of different artists with different styles and had a whole interesting edge to actually market this on. 

but now, paid adverts might as well be money you set on fire, because to be brutally honest, the art looks like shit and the aspect of it being *jigsaw* puzzles which kinda require a lot of finite movements and fittings is gonna make the gameplay a mess. 

i suggest you stop, breathe, and revert back to using real art, not tricking yourself into cheating it and cheaping out on the most integral part of your game's core mechanic and function. then give yourself a proper lead time and do the marketing, with a whole new victory story about how you pulled your project back from the chopping block and gave money to real artists to make work for the game you're so proud of.

replies.author: CraigBMG
replies.body:
To answer the technical questions, after a month of trying to put together a reasonable 3D scene, I realized that rendering an 8K offscreen texture for the puzzle every frame was not going to work on "Mom's laptop GPU," and was also certainly nowhere near the quality of images that I have now.  So, I made the very difficult decision to change direction.

The rest of that is a curiously prejudiced take for a sub ostensibly about exploring generative AI.

replies.author: Atmic
replies.body:
I for one think the art looks pretty damn cool, calming and Zen. I wouldn't give their opinion too much stock, they seem to be pretty caustic. 

I don't think the gameplay hook looks compelling though, at least for me.

I'm not in the target audience likely, but I feel this style of game would work better for mobile with haptics making each puzzle piece snap and feel good. 

Of course tablets can run Steam, and it could definitely work there. It's a hard sell for me.

replies.author: CraigBMG
replies.body: Thanks!  For sure, this is super casual, not a gamer's game!  The mobile space seems even more crowded and even harder to market than Steam, so trying this first.

replies.author: -svde-
replies.body:
i actually provided a pretty damn indepth explanation of exactly what i thought about everything and why. if you think that realistic feedback is caustic, that is your problem. you clearly aren’t proud enough of where you stand on this project to tell people who don’t like the fact that you used AI to fuck off. 

and honestly, i don’t care what you do. use whatever tools you want. i’m not personally attacking  you or harming your work in any way, i’m trying to provide an opinion from a perspective that understands that AI has come and is here to stay, but it isn’t going to completely replace people who actually enjoy creating things on their own, and people are not required to worship the ground you walk on because you know how to type and press a button or two. they’re not even required to be polite about it! 

this may sound “caustic” to you, but i don’t think a lot of y’all understand how fucking whiny and beyond entitled you come off as whenever someone has even the slightest bit of criticism. it’s only children or people with a child’s ignorant mindset that can’t see the forest for the trees. if devs and artists and everyone else have to put up with your grandstanding, then i think you can deal with  little bit of a harsh reality check.

anyway, good luck with your puzzle game. if you aren’t gonna listen to anything  else i said, just idk learn some self confidence and stand behind it.

comments.author: Dont_Bring_Me_Down
comments.body:
This is an AI game dev community. OP used AI as a tool to get a project to a playable state after running into time and technical constraints.

Whether someone personally likes AI or not, that's a completely valid development decision.

Six weeks is also a long time in game development. If OP decides that commissioning new artwork will improve the game or its marketability, then great, there's plenty of time.

But "change it because AI touched it" isn't a design argument.

That decision should be based on whether it makes the game better, not simply because some people may dislike how the art was created.

The hardest part of indie development is actually finishing something. AI or not, the OP got to the finish line, and that's an accomplishment in itself.

Good luck with the launch, OP. 

I hope you keep gathering feedback, improve what you think genuinely needs improving, and get the game in front of players.

comments.author: Playistheway
comments.body:
I think there is a right way and a wrong way to incorporate AI into commercial products, and you've opted for the wrong way.

There is nothing unique here. You're just shipping "curated" images with a simple facade of being a jigsaw puzzle.

There is no market demand for this, so there is no point spending money on advertising.

comments.author: Ahenian
comments.body: As far as I'm aware if you launch with a non-existent wishlist into steam your game will just be buried by the algorithm unless it's a beast of a game that word of mouth takes over. You should always be marketing because gaining traction and an audience takes months, the "overnight" successes basically built their audiences over years, see road to vostok.
